name: Pedro Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Pedro. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead framer for a company that builds custom family houses out in the new suburbs. Framing is the skeleton of the house: walls, floors, roof, all in timber. I run a crew of four, we're on site at seven, and on a good week we'll stand up a whole storey. Then on weekends I do my own jobs, decks and pergolas for people in the area, which is where the real fun is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes the weekend jobs fun, and what tires you out in the week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my own jobs I get to try stuff. I use AI every day, for quotes, for 3D sketches I can show the customer on my phone, even for working out the cut list so I waste less timber. I've got a little side page with photos and the bookings mostly come from there. What tires me out in the week is waiting: for the inspector, for the truss delivery, for someone in the office to approve something I could have sorted in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Sure, possible. I'd still use it for my quotes, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool and that's all, use it for what it's good at. Online I'd probably post one of my 3D deck sketches and say this is what AI is actually good for, nothing more. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a tiny bit bored, honestly. I like new stuff, and I was kind of hoping it'd shake things up in a way I could ride. But money-wise, it changes nothing for me, I've got good pay, a year saved, and the weekend jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing exactly what I'm doing. I'd probably grow the weekend business a bit, take on more decks next summer, maybe hire a helper for Saturdays. I'd keep using the AI tools because they already save me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, like the season ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the weekend work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last summer, about eleven thousand after materials, from maybe fourteen jobs. It's not a fortune, but it paid for the van upgrade. Lina says I work too many Saturdays, and she's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at your main job be glad about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss, Mr. Brandt, for sure. He's 60, he's been framing houses the same way since forever. He keeps saying computers can't swing a hammer, and in this picture he gets to keep saying it.

S0.say: AI is a handy tool and that's all, so use it for what it's good at. He'd post a 3D deck sketch as an example of what it really does well.
S0.think: He'd be a little bored, having hoped for a shake-up he could ride. Financially nothing changes, with good pay, a year of savings and his weekend business.
S0.do: Carries on as now and grows the weekend deck business, maybe hiring a Saturday helper. Keeps using AI tools that already save him hours.
S0.feel: Calm but a bit flat, like a season that ended early.
S0.quote: Lina says I work too many Saturdays, and she's probably right.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is an energetic early adopter who finds the calm scenario slightly disappointing. His weekend business gives him a second income and a place to experiment. He talks about money openly and in specifics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the good one, if you ask me. Change you can actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn it now, don't wait. The guys who use the tools will get the work and the guys who don't will moan about it. I'd probably post something like that, maybe a bit nicer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is great for me. I'm already the guy who does his quotes with AI, so I'd be ahead. The only thing is, if it gets too easy for everyone to sketch and quote, my edge on the weekend jobs shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small CNC router for the weekend work, around six or seven thousand, so I can cut custom brackets and railings myself. I'd sign up for any training my company offered on new site software, and I'd offer to be the one who tests it. I'd also look at turning the weekend thing into a proper registered business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge might shrink. What would you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Find the next edge. Maybe I'd go into stuff that's harder to copy, like curved timber or outdoor kitchens. There's always something the average guy isn't doing yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Tomasz, he's great on a nail gun but hates phones. But he's 30 and smart, he'd get there if someone sat with him. I'd try to be that someone, if I'm honest.

S1.say: Learn the tools now, because people who use them will get the work and people who don't will complain. He'd post something like that, a little more politely.
S1.think: It's great for him since he already quotes with AI, though easier tools for everyone could shrink his edge on weekend jobs.
S1.do: Buys a small CNC router for six or seven thousand to cut custom parts, volunteers to test new site software, and looks at registering his weekend work as a proper business.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro is the most entrepreneurial voice so far: he thinks in terms of edges and staying ahead. He'd invest his own money quickly. He's also willing to help a crewmate who's less comfortable with technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, whoa. That's a different game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it's going to be rough and people need help to get through it, the government has to do something sensible, fast. But I'd also say don't freeze, start moving. That's what I'd tell my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be okay at first and then not sure. If robots can frame a house, my main job is gone, and if AI can do 3D sketches and quotes, so is my weekend edge. But I've got no kids, a year of savings, and I can learn fast, so I'd jump to whatever needs people next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning to set up and fix construction robots straight away, online and with whatever company is bringing them in. I'd look for jobs with the firms that make or rent the robots, even if it meant moving to another city where they're based. Lina's a dental hygienist, she can work anywhere, so we'd go where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a lot, but I'd be more wired than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move cities. What would make you decide to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real job offer, with a salary I can check. If one of the robot firms said come be a field technician for a year, I'd be packing the van that weekend. Lina would want a say, of course, and she'd probably insist on seeing the apartment first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound quite relaxed for the fastest scenario. Is there a part that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, the part after. If it really can do almost anything, then fixing robots is just another thing it can do, eventually. I'd be ahead for a while and then I'd be in the same spot as everyone. I try not to think too far down that road.

S2.say: It will be rough and the government must help sensibly and fast, but people shouldn't freeze. He'd tell his crew to start moving.
S2.think: He'd be fine at first, then unsure, since robots could take his framing and AI his weekend edge. With no kids, a year of savings and fast learning, he'd jump to whatever needs people next.
S2.do: Starts learning to set up and repair construction robots right away and looks for jobs with robot makers or rental firms. Moves city with his partner Lina if that's where the work is.
S2.quote: If one of the robot firms said come be a field technician for a year, I'd be packing the van that weekend.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario Pedro's first move is toward the technology. His lack of children, savings and a partner with a portable job make moving easy. He admits the long-term worry but chooses not to dwell on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can plan around properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty to get ready if you start now, so start now. Companies should be training their crews and government should make it easy to switch. I'd keep it simple like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is perfect for someone like me. I'd have time to build the weekend business up and get trained on the robots. By the time it arrives, I could be the guy who runs a small robot framing crew of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd register the business and start saving for equipment. By year three I'd probably lease my first framing robot, if they exist by then, and offer faster builds to small builders like Mr. Brandt. I'd keep my main job until the business could pay both me and a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr. Brandt if you pitched him a robot crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you don't have to buy one, just hire me and mine for the frame and keep your guys for the finishing. He'd grumble, but he likes saving money more than he likes complaining. I think he'd go for it after a couple of houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Tomasz and the others on your crew in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want at least one of them with me, probably Tomasz, as the guy on the ground checking the robot's work. The others, I don't know. That's the part of it I don't feel good about.

S3.say: Five years is plenty if you start now, so companies should train crews and the government should make switching easy.
S3.think: Five years is perfect for him to grow the weekend business and get trained on robots. He pictures running a small robot framing crew of his own.
S3.do: Registers the business in year one and saves for equipment, then leases a framing robot around year three to offer faster frames to small builders. Keeps his main job until the business can pay him and a helper.
S3.quote: He'd grumble, but he likes saving money more than he likes complaining.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Pedro shifts from employee to robot-crew owner. His pragmatic centre outlook shows in focusing on what works rather than who to blame. He's honest that he doesn't feel good about the crewmates he couldn't bring along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone not being ready after ten years' warning. Learn something, try something. And government should keep it fair so people aren't left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good about it. Ten years is enough to try two or three things and see what sticks. Maybe the robot crew, maybe something totally different, like designing outdoor spaces with AI and having robots build them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, I'd keep the main job, grow the weekend business and do a course in design software. I'd buy into the robot side once the machines were proven on a few real sites, not the first ones. Somewhere around year five, I'd probably go full-time on my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, kind of looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lina change any plans with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd buy a place sooner, while I'm still on good wages and the bank likes my payslips. We rent right now. And kids are a maybe, later, but that's not really a robot question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for robots to be proven on a few sites first. That's more cautious than you've been so far. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years there's no prize for going first. With two years you have to jump. With ten you can let someone else make the expensive mistakes and then buy the second-generation machine cheaper.

S4.say: With ten years' warning, nobody has an excuse not to be ready, but the government should keep it fair so people aren't left behind.
S4.think: He'd feel good, with time to try two or three paths, such as a robot crew or designing outdoor spaces with AI and having robots build them.
S4.do: Keeps his main job for a few years while growing the weekend business and studying design software. Buys into robots once proven on real sites and goes full-time on his own business around year five.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to it.
S4.quote: With ten you can let someone else make the expensive mistakes and then buy the second-generation machine cheaper.
S4.fieldNote: An interesting turn: with more time, the early adopter becomes deliberately patient, which he explains in clear cost terms. He would also consider buying a home sooner while his payslips are strong. His outlook is optimistic and practical rather than ideological.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even I can't learn fast enough to stay ahead forever in that one. What would help is training on the robots that's quick and cheap, run by the companies bringing them in, and some help for people who need to move cities to follow the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what customers will want. I think some people will pay more for a deck that a guy built by hand, like they pay more for homemade bread. Nobody asks the customers.

headlineQuote: There's always something the average guy isn't doing yet.
portrait: Pedro Wagner is a 27-year-old lead framer on custom suburban houses who runs a weekend deck and pergola business using AI for quotes, 3D sketches and cut lists. He finds the AI Plateau a little dull and sees Steady Disruption as a chance to invest in a CNC router and grow the side business. Even AGI by 2028 leaves him only uneasy: he'd retrain on robots and move cities with his partner Lina to follow the work, though he admits his lead would only be temporary. With five or ten years he plans to own a small robot crew or a design business, and becomes more patient as the time grows.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even he couldn't learn fast enough to stay ahead for long.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, cheap robot training run by the companies bringing the machines in, plus help for people who need to move cities to follow the work.
